brief.head: Surplus on the map
brief.text: Free Google Maps, Ajay Shah said, generates a phenomenal consumer surplus. He once blogged asking whether India’s GDP went up by 0.1 per cent when navigation arrived. {#gdp}

brief.head: No map does it all
brief.text: Google Maps won’t show a district boundary, Ajay Shah said, so if your unit is the district, it is the wrong map. Every map is a model of the world. {044-C04}

brief.head: The anti-Google club
brief.text: When Apple locked iPod music into its own format, Ajay Shah said, rivals rallied round MP3. Now Microsoft and Amazon back OpenStreetMap against Google. {044-C10}

brief.head: Spin round Nanda Devi
brief.text: Install the desktop version of Google Earth, Ajay Shah urged, on a big screen in terrain mode. Rotate around Nanda Devi, “visualizing where the plutonium might be hiding”. {044-J06}

brief.head: Emperor of everything
brief.text: Shah Jahan, Ajay Shah recalled, was more or less convinced that he ruled most of the world. “That’s the main character syndrome in a geographical sense,” said Amit Varma. {044-J02}

thought.text: The way that a map is made, that’s the way a person is made.
thought.who: Amit Varma, finding a lesson for life in the patient work of surveyors

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on how India got its maps
lead.head: From Everest to everywhere
body: Picture yourself as Akbar or Aurangzeb, Ajay Shah said: an emperor who doesn’t know much about the country he rules. How do you get from A to B? Where do you ford a river, wage a war or build a road?
“There are just thousands of questions,” Shah said, “and frankly, you’re just in the dark.”

Maps, he argued, take you from that darkness to the light. That was the thread of an hour in which Amit Varma drew out one of Shah’s great loves, from a British survey of 1767 to the phone in your pocket.
## From Clive to Everest
Map-making came to India with the British, Shah said, when Robert Clive commissioned it in 1767. George Everest later surveyed the whole country, and the Survey of India came out of that work.
A map, Shah insisted, is not a painting but data. “It’s a list of coordinates which have certain properties.” {044-C02}

Surveying is costly, but once it is done, each extra copy costs almost nothing. That makes maps a public good, and Shah was blunt about whom it serves: “We don’t give a damn about what the state has in their pocket.” {044-C03}

Free India, he said, let the work slide. In many regions, he believes, the last survey dates from around 1934. The sheets were coarse, and maps near the border and the coast could not be sold at all, for fear of terrorists.
He does not single out one agency. Monetary policy, the police, the judiciary, the military and the statistical system all work badly, he said: it is “a part of this underdevelopment”.
## Maps from orbit

Then technology changed everything. GPS, satellite photographs, synthetic aperture radar, elevation maps and the traces of millions of Android phones did away with the need to walk the land with a theodolite. {044-C06}
On these, Shah said, three systems have been built: Google Maps, Google Earth and OpenStreetMap. “The people of India are now in a map paradise the likes of which we have never seen before.”
It is, he said, an end run around India’s whole problem of state capacity, built on public goods paid for by taxpayers in rich countries. {044-C07}
Varma, reading Jorge Luis Borges’s parable of a map as big as its empire, added that Google Maps escapes the trap of the static map by updating itself as the world moves.
## Despair, and hope
For Varma, the lesson reached beyond maps. He said he is full of despair about the state of the world, and that technology is the one thing that gives him hope. {044-C12}

Shah added a caution. The Indian state’s first instinct, he said, has been to ban citizens’ map-making, with terrorism as the excuse for almost anything. Technology needs a liberal pushback against the coercive state to go with it.
Varma went further: the lines on a map are man-made, and history shows they do not last.
Then Varma set his co-host a map quiz. “An exam. An exam. I love exams,” Shah said. “Even if I get zero on five.”
He recognised Middle-earth at once, mistook George Orwell’s *1984* for a map of malaria and guessed fertility rate for linguistic diversity, on which India leads the world.
The last map, of the heights of 19-year-old men, put India near the bottom. That, the hosts agreed, is about nutrition and illness, not genes.

second.label: Property rights
second.head: Toilets by satellite
second.deck: Old Google Earth images won tribals their land, and changed their incentives
body: Barun Mitra and his fellow activists were fighting for tribal land rights, in Gujarat as Amit Varma remembers it. Varma called it one of the most inspiring stories he had heard, told in the documentary *India Awakes*. {044-R06}

The tribals had no proof that they had occupied the land long enough to qualify. So the activists went back in time with historical Google Earth satellite images, used them as evidence in court, and won. Ajay Shah added that the team walked the ground with Garmin handheld GPS units.
In all their years on the land, the tribals had built few pakka structures and no toilets in their homes. Once the right was theirs, they built toilets. {044-S03}

quote.text: But the moment they had the land right, the incentive changed, and they built toilets.

second.caption: the tribals’ satellite evidence

third.head: Shorter, without shrinking
body: At college, Ajay Shah was tall for his generation. Today he is short beside 20- and 25-year-olds. His height has not changed; the people around him have grown taller. {044-S08}
“That’s the economic development and the improvements of India within my life,” he said, “that I’ve gone from being a reasonably tall person to being a reasonably short person.”

It came up in Amit Varma’s map quiz, whose last map showed the heights of 19-year-old men. Height owes almost nothing to genetics, Shah said: people of Indian descent raised in advanced economies reach the same average height. {044-C14} Each childhood illness interrupts the use of growth hormone.
Varma had seen it himself. On Bombay’s local trains in the mid-1990s, he noticed that people in first class were taller than people in second. Anecdotal, he admitted, but stark. {044-S09}
third.caption: going from tall to short

p2.title: Darkness to light
p2.deck: How India went from Akbar’s guesswork to a map paradise, by way of George Everest and Google. {#paradise}

sections.label: Before maps
sections.head: Water for horses, or a ford?
sections.caption: the emperor in the dark
body: In the Middle Ages, Ajay Shah said, even an emperor ruled in the dark. Akbar and Aurangzeb had no way to plan a route, judge a country’s revenue or decide where a settlement might go.

What they had was local knowledge, held in local languages and garbled in translation like Chinese whispers. “There will be all kinds of confusion when Tulu is translated into Persian,” he said. One man asks where to water his horses; the other hears, where can the horses ford the river? {044-J01}

Natives might withhold what they knew, want a rent for it or deliberately mislead the traveller. With only local information, Shah said, you are always solving local problems, never seeing the bird’s-eye picture.
## Boom, you know the answer
Maps “abruptly take you from darkness to the light”, Shah said. You bumble around asking people, then you look at a map “and boom, you know the answer”.

Precision is the point. On a 1:10,000 hiking sheet, each centimetre is 100 metres; with a compass, the map becomes your guide. A good map, Shah said, means you don’t need a local tracker at all. {#tracker}
~ Amit Varma answered with lines from the Magnetic Fields song *The Book of Love*. {044-R02} Love, Shah replied, is as much a mystery as ever; our understanding of space has been transformed.

quote.text: So you don’t need to be a local, it is a way of banging away at the nativism that otherwise every region suffers from.

sections.label: The British survey
sections.head: A triangle at a time
sections.caption: the first maps of India
body: Maps came to India with the British, Ajay Shah said, as early as 1767, “a scant ten years after the Battle of Plassey”. Robert Clive commissioned the work in the parts of Bengal and Bihar they controlled. {044-J16}

The great explosion came with George Everest. His teams covered the country in interlocking triangles, about 30 km a side as Shah recalled, and found along the way that the peak now called Mount Everest was India’s highest point.
## Data, not paintings
A printed map, Shah said, is only a painting made out of data: a list of coordinates with properties attached. {044-C02}

Surveying a country is enormously costly; once it is done, each extra copy costs next to nothing. That makes maps a classic public good, Shah said, and such a good is worth nothing if the state keeps it to itself. {044-C03}

Amit Varma drew a human lesson. The surveyor noting the height of hills never saw the big picture; he probably never saw the finished map. Varma quoted the novelist E.L. Doctorow: “If you can see the light from your headlights, you can make the whole distance that way.” {044-J18}
~ Shah drew the same moral from decades of patient survey work: keep building and don’t ask for gratification. “Don’t look at the number of likes on your Instagram post.” {044-C05}

quote.text: A public good is for the people. It’s not there for the state.

sections.label: From the sky
sections.head: Orbiters that only shout
sections.caption: the end of the theodolite
body: A friend once told Amit Varma that people born today will never know what it is to be lost. Varma called it a mind-blowing thought. {044-S05}

Ajay Shah explained how it happened. The old way needed British levels of state capability: thousands of people walking the country with theodolites, “accurately jotting down coordinates”. Four technologies changed that.

The first is GPS. The US Department of Defense keeps 44 satellites aloft, Shah said, and they never talk to your phone. The handset hears a few of them and works out its own position, to about 10 metres. {044-C06}
## Tracing paper in orbit
The second is satellite imagery. Shah likened it to the translucent paper children lay over a picture: trace the roads and buildings on a satellite photograph, and you have a first draft of a map.

The third is synthetic aperture radar, which shows every building in 3D; Shah wants to devote a whole episode to it one day. {#sar} The fourth is the digital elevation map, which estimates the height of every place.
Add the GPS traces of Android phones, Shah said, and it all adds up to a technological revolution.
~ GPS alone, Shah said, is more accurate than most theodolite trigonometry a human map-maker could manage, though its estimate of elevation is less precise.

quote.text: All they do is shout. They only broadcast. That’s all. And they don’t know the existence of a handset.

sections.label: Map paradise
sections.head: Free, as of today
sections.caption: Google Maps, Google Earth and OSM
body: Reforming the Survey of India, Ajay Shah said, would take a generation of visionary leaders. Instead, three systems have given Indians better maps than George Everest ever had.
The first is Google Maps, “a madly great map”, free to users, Shah noted, “as of today”.
Amit Varma brought in Jorge Luis Borges’s *On Exactitude in Science*, the parable of cartographers whose map of the empire was the size of the empire. {044-R05}
Such a map would be out of date the next moment, Varma said. Google Maps gets round that by updating itself, rerouting him on the way from Andheri to Bandra East as traffic changes. {044-C08}
## Delight on a desktop

“It is delight. It is paradise,” Shah said of the desktop version of Google Earth, the second system. The third is OpenStreetMap, which Shah called the true digital public good, built by volunteers with no coercion and no taxation. {044-C09}
None of it used Indian tax money or Indian state capacity. “It’s like an end run around the entire state capacity problem of getting the Survey of India to work,” Shah said. {044-C07}
~ Varma pitched a film about two OSM volunteers who meet at a mapping meetup and go map-making together. Things go wrong, but it ends well: the film is called *Awesome*. {044-J07}

quote.text: It is non-rival, it is non-excludable, it is the digital public good.

sections.label: The one hope
sections.head: Lines that won’t last
sections.caption: technology and the coercive state
body: Amit Varma drew a cautionary tale from the story. Too many of us take the world as fixed, he said: we assume the state must make the maps, and that the state is moribund.
He is full of despair about the state of the world, he said, but technology gives him hope. {044-C12} Even the smartphone, for all its surveillance and distraction, gives people freedom.

Ajay Shah put it another way: “Our equipment is better than Satyajit Ray. It is our imaginations that are the constraint.” Varma granted the equipment, but added that no one is better than Satyajit Ray. {044-J09}
## The ban reflex

Then Shah’s own caution. Faced with citizens making their own maps, the Indian state’s first instinct has been to ban it: private mapping, Google Street View, foreign satellite imagery. “You can ban anything under the excuse of terrorism,” he said. {044-C11}
Technology alone is not enough, he argued: it needs “a large dose of liberal philosophy”.
Varma wondered whether, after the crumbling of the mainstream in media and entertainment, nation states might be next. The lines on a map, he said, are man-made and temporary. {044-C13}
~ Shah has walked to the edge of the India-China border in Ladakh and in Uttarakhand. “It’s just Himalaya,” he said. “There is no line on the map.”

quote.text: All of those lines are temporary. They are man made and they’re temporary, that’s what we’ve seen through history. Nothing is permanent.

side.boxText: George Everest led the survey that first mapped India, and chose a house in Mussoorie overlooking a forested valley. Ajay Shah’s pick, John Keay’s *The Great Arc*, tells the story of the early Survey of India: “a heroic tale”. {#greatarc}

contQuote.text: Because I think technology can build the sort of liberal world we believe in, and I mean in the classical liberal sense, technology can empower individuals in a way that political movements have failed to do.

p3.title: Tales from the map room
p3.deck: Kept, banned, traced and pasted on a wall: four stories of maps

stories.start: In Masurri, there was a beautiful thing which was called Everest House
stories.end: who led this amazing project on building the first maps for India
stories.caption: Everest House in Mussoorie
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on his favourite ruin, and what became of it
stories.head: A bungalow before the makeover
body: When George Everest had to choose a place to live, Ajay Shah said, he would have chosen the most amazing spot. He picked one in Mussoorie, overlooking a valley where, Shah seems to remember, tigers roamed in those days.
This was the man whose teams had built the first map of the country, and whose name went to India’s highest point. The house came to be called Everest House.
Many years later it was a run-down old white marble house, tangled in legal disputes and in a state of decay and disrepair. Yet it was open to the whole public: anybody could just go there.

Shah loved it. He would sit there, thinking and dreaming. “You could feel what it was like to be George Everest,” he said, “to have built the first map of this country, and then to be living in that bungalow on the edge of that valley and the forest.” {044-S01}
“It was just absolutely atmospheric,” he said. “My mind would just go wild with the feeling of that place.”

He tells it in the past tense, and the reason is a sad one. On his last visit, some government agencies were doing ugly and tasteless construction to turn the house into a museum. “Unfortunately, it was just ugly.”
~ “These things should really be done by people who have taste,” Shah said. {#taste} Those who saw the house before, he added, may remember it as it was.
stories.why: Some places carry history best when left alone. Restoring heritage takes taste as well as money, and an official makeover can destroy the very atmosphere that made a place worth visiting.

stories.start: by the time I came to the age of yearning for maps
stories.end: whatever treasure trove of maps they have was not there for the people
stories.caption: the maps India wouldn’t sell
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Survey of India’s forbidden sheets
stories.head: Wanted in Bombay, kept in London
body: When Ajay Shah came to the age of yearning for maps, he discovered some very irritating things. Many Survey of India sheets were outdated; in many regions, he believes, the last survey was from 1934 or so. {#lastsurvey}
Nor was the scale right. A walker wants 1:10,000 or 1:20,000; the Survey sold 1:200,000, where a centimetre is two kilometres. Those sheets were “nice, but just unsatisfying”.

Then, “to add insult to injury”, maps within some 100 km of the border, coastline included, could not be sold, lest terrorists use them. Living in Bombay, Shah was cut off from the coast; hiking in the Himalayas, from the border. {044-S02}
~ Yet every Survey of India map, he said, is in a museum in London. “So any self-respecting terrorist will go to London and get those maps.” {044-J03}
stories.why: A security rule can take a public good from the citizens who paid for it while barely slowing a real adversary. As Ajay Shah put it, “what you end up doing is shooting yourself in the foot”.

stories.start: The second stage is Google has human beings, by the way.
stories.end: all those things are visible from the photographs from space
stories.caption: Google’s map room in Hyderabad
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how the world’s map came to be drawn in India
stories.head: Made in Hyderabad, for the world
body: Google started out thinking, Ajay Shah said, that where a government released map data, as in the United States and the UK, its work was done.

That approach didn’t scale to countries like India, where the government either doesn’t have the data or won’t release it. Sanjay Jain, a pioneer at Google, pushed the company to up its game. {044-S06}

Jain and others wrote software, called MapMaker as Shah recalls. A large facility went up in Hyderabad, where some 5,000 to 10,000 people, he believes, trace roads, bridges, buildings and rivers from satellite photographs.
~ Then come the traces from Android phones. If a phone moves at 60 kph, Shah said, “that’s a motorable road”. {#motorable} Shah urged listeners to switch off location tracking all the same.

quote.text: So they upped their game saying, No, we will make the map for the whole world.

stories.end: I've just not been able to find a good wall-sized map of India
stories.caption: his father’s wall-sized map
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the map that started a lifelong love
stories.head: Four sheets, one country, one boy
body: In Ajay Shah’s childhood home there was a map twice his height. His father had pasted the four Survey of India sheets that made up the country onto a wooden board and fixed it to the wall.

The boy could not stop looking. “I just constantly would look at that and try to get a sense of the land and understand each river,” Shah said. He tried to mug up every district and place name, and worked out the best routes. {044-S04}
“It was a treat.” Ever since, he has looked for a good modern wall-sized map of India, of National Geographic or Rand McNally quality, and not found one.
~ So he appealed to his audience: gentle reader, if you know of one, tell him. {#wallmap}
stories.why: A small act by a parent can start a lifelong passion. And even now, something as simple as a good wall map of India is hard to find: Shah has looked ever since, and found none.

quiz.q: Who commissioned Britain’s first map-making in India, and how soon after Plassey?
quiz.a: Robert Clive, in 1767, a scant ten years after the battle.

quiz.q: Why could Ajay Shah not buy Survey of India maps of Bombay’s coast?
quiz.a: Maps within about 100 km of the border or coast were banned, citing terrorists.

quiz.q: Where, by Shah’s account, does Google trace its map of the whole world?
quiz.a: In a large facility in Hyderabad, with perhaps 5,000 to 10,000 people.

quiz.q: What evidence won tribal land rights in the case Amit Varma described?
quiz.a: Historical Google Earth satellite images, which let the activists go back in time.

quiz.q: In the Borges parable Varma read out, how big was the empire’s map?
quiz.a: As big as the empire itself, coinciding with it point for point.

quiz.q: In Varma’s map quiz, what did Shah mistake George Orwell’s *1984* map for?
quiz.a: A map of malaria or yellow fever, before Varma revealed Oceania and Eurasia.
